PROJECT NO. 58482​    ​            ​      § ​    ​      BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITY
LARGE LOAD DEMAND ​ ​              ​      §​     ​      COMMISSION OF TEXAS
MANAGEMENT SERVICE ​ ​             ​      §



Submitted by: Cyrus Reed, Legislative and Conservation Director,
cyrus.reed@sierraclub.org, 512-888-9411

Comments of the Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club

The Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club appreciates the opportunity to provide
comments on the proposed rule to implement a “Large Load Demand Management
Service” as required by SB 6. As a supporter of SB 6, we recognize that creating such a
service does create a cost to the whole market, but believe the benefit of having such a
service specifically for emergency situations driven by extreme weather conditions or
events will be of general benefit to the grid. We hope that large loads that are not
otherwise participating in other demand response services, including market-driven
price response behavior, will participate. We also support allowing an individual large
load to “separate” their facility in such a way that one part of the facility could be
price-responsive while another could be qualified for the LLDMS service. Still, we want
the service to be well defined, cost-effective and limited in its use. We view this new
service as a kind of hybrid between a contract service like Emergency Response Service
and a more market-based ancillary service. Because it would only be deployed in
defined situations, it can not be treated as strictly a day-ahead ancillary service, but we
also don’t think it is a “capacity” product where those qualified to provide the LLDMS
would be in a long-term contract with ERCOT. Before turning to some general comments
on the rule itself, we wanted to provide brief answers to the questions put forward by
staff.


                                                                                         1
 Responses to staff Questions


    1.​ Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling
entity representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to
deploy but is subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand
Management Service (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer
that is available but not ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS
obligation period be compensated some percentage of the market clearing pricing
for the large load customer 's availability to reduce demand during the LLDMS
obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate payment to the large load
customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation period?

We do not believe that SB 6 authorized or contemplated payments for availability, but
for actual deployment. Thus, unlike some aspects of ERS, which pay facilities to be
available as needed, we view the LLDMS as a pay-for-performance service. Ultimately,
all loads will pay for thai service, and we would prefer that large loads that participate
are paid for their service, not for simply being available. While we could see the need for
a small payment for testing and qualification purposes, we would not want the market
to be paying for availability. If the PUCT does move forward with availability verification
payments, it should be limited to 10% of market-clearing pricing.


   2.​ Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a
calendar year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?


The budget should be set on a yearly basis, based in part on the experience of the
service. For many years, the ERS budget at ERCOT was limited to $50 million before it
was recently raised to $75 million post-Uri. That budget does allow some flexibility since
ERCOT can raise it from $75 million to $100 million.

We would suggest a similar process. Because LLDMS is a new service, we think
perhaps starting with a $50 million budget cap, with some flexibility to go up to $75
million if needed in an emergency would be appropriate. The budgetary amount could
be adjusted as needed through ERCOT and Commission action. The budgetary cap is
important to consumers because it creates an upper limit on potential expenses, and
allows load service entities the opportunity to adjust rates and expectations as needed.

   3.​ What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and

                                                                                          2
 how far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

SB 6 requires a minimum of 24-hour notice for any LLDMS deployment to allow
qualifying large loads to participate. Because the statute implementing the LLDMS is
geared to weather emergencies - unusual events that could have major impacts on large
geographic areas - we think ERCOT should avoid using a cadence that is too far in
advance and could create expectations for deployment. Thus, monthly predictions are
probably too far in advance. We would suggest a two to five day predictive tool - so
48-hour to 120-hours - is an appropriate amount of time to order potential deployment
of the service.


    4.​ Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If
so, what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

We do not believe that LLDMS was intended for transmission emergencies unless those
transmission emergencies are directly related to extreme weather events. If the PUCT or
ERCOT is to allow such use of LLDMS for transmission events it should be tied to
unusual weather events that impact transmission. In general, we do not favor the use of
LLDMS for transmission emergencies, which seems outside the scope of the intent of
SB 6.


Comments on the proposed rule itself

The Sierra Club is in general support of the proposed rule to implement LLDMS with a
few exceptions.

Definitions

We are concerned that the definitions establish an expectation that LLDMS would be
used for transmission emergencies, which seems outside the scope of SB 6. We would
suggest removing it or modifying it to be related to transmission emergencies directly
related to weather conditions.

Transmission emergency -- A condition in which an element on the transmission system
is operating above its emergency rating because of an extreme weather condition such
that it creates a significant risk of firm load shed.

Ineligibility




                                                                                         3
 First, as mentioned Sierra Club favors some flexibility in allowing a large load that can
do so, to be able to separate its facility in a way that allows part of it to participate in the
LLMDS even if another part participates in one of the services mentioned in (2)
Inegibility. Thus while we support the list of programs for which a large load would be
ineligible we would consider adding some language such as

(2) (J) “With approval by ERCOT, a large load may qualify part of its load for LLDMS, and
allow for one part of its load to participate in the LLDMS service, even if another part of
its load participates in one of the other services listed in (A)-(I).”

Procurement

While we have no specific changes, we are concerned that monthly probabilistic
modeling might lead to an over-procurement of LLDMS, and trust that ERCOT would rely
more generally on predictive models closer to the event. We do not object to the
language around rejection of procurement though we are unsure if a maximum level of
$5,000 per MWh (the System Wide Offer Cap) will be sufficient to invite participation.
ERCOT could consider a slightly higher value such as 2X the System Offer Cap.
Presumably, this service will only be provided by large loads that are not
price-responsive and it is unclear what level of payment will be needed to secure
service.

Payment and Charges

We are opposed to paying large loads for availability as suggested in the draft rule and
believe it is not supported by the statute. However, if it remains we would suggest
limiting it to 10% of the market clearing price.

In terms of the proposed budget we would suggest the following language which would
be consistent with the way that ERS is handled, where there is discretion to go above
the annual limit if needed. Suggested language can be found below:

(4) ERCOT may spend a maximum of $50 million in procurement costs during a
calendar year, except that in a weather emergency ERCOT may exceed the budget by
up to $25 million with PUCT approval.


The Sierra Club appreciates the opportunity to make these brief comments.




                                                                                               4
 Comments of the Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club: Executive Summary

Sierra Club is generally supportive of the staff’s proposed rule, which we believe
implements a required component of SB 6. However, we have a few suggested
improvements or changes in the proposed rule. These include:

   1.​ Eliminate or refine the use of LLDMS for transmission emergencies to tie it
       specifically to weather emergencies;
   2.​ Allow for a large load to separate a part of its load to provide LLDMS even if other
       parts of its load participate in a different service that would normally make it
       ineligible;
   3.​ Adopt an annual budget of $50 million, but allow for the budget cap to rise up to
       $75 million in an emergency with ERCOT and PUCT approval.
   4.​ Allow some flexibility on the $5,000 per MWh payment, such as considering 2X
       the System-Wide Offer Cap to invite more participation;
   5.​ Eliminate payments for “availability,” or if not limit it to 10% of the market clearing
       price.

In terms of the cadence of procurement of LLDMS, we would avoid using a monthly
probabilistic model, and focus on procurement some 2 to 5 days out of an expected
emergency weather event, which should provide adequate time to meet the 24-hour
statutory deadline.
